derivations.claim: Choose a positively oriented orthonormal coframe $e^1,e^2,e^3,e^4$ of $V^*$. The defining wedge identity gives $*_g e^{12}=e^{34}$, $*_g e^{13}=-e^{24}$, $*_g e^{14}=e^{23}$, $*_g e^{23}=e^{14}$, $*_g e^{24}=-e^{13}$, and $*_g e^{34}=e^{12}$. Thus $*_g$ permutes the orthonormal basis of $\Lambda^2V^*$ with signs, so it is an isometry; applying it twice to each of the six basis vectors gives $*_g^2=I$. The same conclusions hold after tensoring each basis vector with any member of an orthonormal basis of $W$.

For $\Phi^+=\tfrac12(\Phi+*_g\Phi)$ and $\Phi^-=\tfrac12(\Phi-*_g\Phi)$, the identity $*_g^2=I$ from step 1.1 gives $*_g\Phi^+=\Phi^+$, $*_g\Phi^-=-\Phi^-$, and $\Phi=\Phi^++\Phi^-$. If $*_g\alpha=\alpha$ and $*_g\beta=-\beta$, the isometry property from step 1.1 gives $\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle=\langle *_g\alpha,*_g\beta\rangle=-\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle$, hence $\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle=0$. The decomposition is unique because the intersection of the two eigenspaces is zero.

Under $\widehat g=\lambda^2g$, the induced inner product on $\Lambda^2V^*$ scales by $\lambda^{-4}$ because each covector factor scales by $\lambda^{-2}$, while the oriented volume form scales by $\lambda^4$. Hence for all $\alpha,\beta\in\Lambda^2V^*$, $\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_{\widehat g}\,\mathrm{vol}_{\widehat g}=\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_g\,\mathrm{vol}_g$. The defining wedge identity therefore gives $\alpha\wedge *_{\widehat g}\beta=\alpha\wedge *_g\beta$ for every $\alpha$; nondegeneracy of the wedge pairing between two-forms in dimension four implies $*_{\widehat g}\beta=*_g\beta$. The identity extends $W$-linearly.

Let $G$ be a finite-dimensional real Lie group, $M$ a smooth manifold, and $P$
a smooth manifold. A **smooth right principal $G$-bundle** is a right principal
$G$-bundle $\pi:P\to M$ in the topological sense of
[[def-principal-g-bundle-and-associated-fiber-bundle]], with the following
additional smooth structure: $\pi$ and the right $G$-action are smooth, and
the principal-bundle charts can be chosen as equivariant diffeomorphisms
$\pi^{-1}(U)\cong U\times G$. Thus each chart respects the projection to
$U$ and the right action on the $G$ factor. The smoothness convention is that
of [[def-smooth-map-between-manifolds-with-boundary]]; boundaryless manifolds
are the default in this item.

The topological principal-bundle clause retains its free, transitive right
action on every fibre and its local triviality. Smoothness adds compatible
differentiable structure; it does not select a connection or assert that a
global trivialization exists. The empty-base case is allowed and then $P$ is
empty by the cited topological definition.

A **finite-dimensional real Lie group** is a group $G$, in the sense of
[[def-group]], together with the structure of a finite-dimensional real smooth
manifold such that the maps

$$m:G\times G\longrightarrow G,\qquad m(g,h)=gh,$$

and

$$\operatorname{inv}:G\longrightarrow G,\qquad \operatorname{inv}(g)=g^{-1},$$

are smooth in the sense of
[[def-smooth-map-between-manifolds-with-boundary]]. Its identity element is
denoted by $e$ (or occasionally $1$).

Unless an item explicitly says otherwise, every Lie group on this page is real,
finite-dimensional, and has no manifold boundary. Dimension zero is allowed;
for example, any countable discrete group with its discrete zero-dimensional
smooth structure is a Lie group. A Lie group cannot be empty because a group
contains its identity. The definition applies unchanged in dimension one,
uses no metric or nondegeneracy hypothesis, and makes no choice from a family
of sets.

derivations.claim: The generated equivalence classes contain one representative from each chart copy exactly when the base point is in $U\cap V$: the transition $(x,h)_V\mapsto(x,\tau(x)h)_U$ is bijective there, with inverse $(x,k)_U\mapsto(x,\tau(x)^{-1}k)_V$ by [F2]. Thus the canonical maps $j_U:U\times G\to P$ and $j_V:V\times G\to P$ are injective. For every open $W\subseteq U\times G$, the preimage of $j_U(W)$ in $Q$ is the open subset $W_U$ together with the inverse transition image of $W|_{(U\cap V)\times G}$ in the $V$ copy; hence $j_U(W)$ is open in the quotient. The same argument applies to $j_V$, so these maps are open embeddings and their images give product charts covering $P$. On their overlap $j_U^{-1}j_V(x,h)=(x,\tau(x)h)$, a diffeomorphism with inverse $(x,k)\mapsto(x,\tau(x)^{-1}k)$ by [F2]. Therefore these product charts define a smooth atlas on $P$.

The induced projection is continuous because the two product projections agree on the equivalence relation. If two points of $P$ project to distinct points of $X$, disjoint base neighborhoods separate them since $X$ is Hausdorff. If they project to the same $x$, choose $U$ or $V$ containing $x$; both points lie in that product chart, where distinct group coordinates have disjoint neighborhoods because the chart is Hausdorff. Hence $P$ is Hausdorff. Each product chart is second-countable, and the union of countable bases from the two charts is a countable base for $P$. The coordinate changes are smooth by step 1.1, so the resulting smooth manifold structure has the required separation and countability properties.

The formula $[x,h]_i\cdot k=[x,hk]_i$ is well-defined because $(x,\tau(x)h)_U\cdot k=(x,\tau(x)hk)_U\sim(x,hk)_V$; associativity and the identity law follow from the group law. In each chart it is the smooth product action by [F2], and it is free and transitive on each fibre because right multiplication on the $G$ coordinate has those properties. By steps 1.1 and 2.1, the charts are smooth product charts and $P$ is Hausdorff and second-countable. The map $\pi$ is smooth and locally the product projection, so [F1] applies and $P\to X$ is a smooth right principal $G$-bundle. The sections $s_U,s_V$ are smooth in these charts, and $[x,e]_V=[x,\tau(x)]_U$ gives $s_V=s_U\tau$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the axiom of countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $M$ be a finite-dimensional, Hausdorff, second-countable smooth manifold without boundary. A **non-Abelian gauge datum on $M$** consists of the following specified objects.

First choose a finite-dimensional real Lie group $G$ that is compact in its manifold topology (every open cover has a finite subcover) and noncommutative (there are $g,h\in G$ with $gh\ne hg$). The actual group $G$, including its global form, is part of the datum. Its Lie algebra is $\mathfrak g=\operatorname{Lie}(G)=T_eG$ with the bracket transported from left-invariant smooth vector fields.

Choose a smooth right principal $G$-bundle $\pi:P\to M$: the projection and right action are smooth, and the action is free and transitive on each fibre. There is an open cover $\{U_\alpha\}_{\alpha\in A}$ of $M$ with a family of equivariant diffeomorphisms $\phi_\alpha:\pi^{-1}(U_\alpha)\to U_\alpha\times G$ for $\alpha\in A$, each over $U_\alpha$. Explicitly, $\operatorname{pr}_1\circ\phi_\alpha=\pi$, and if $\phi_\alpha(p)=(x,g)$ then $\phi_\alpha(ph)=(x,gh)$ for every $h\in G$.

Choose a specified set $I$ of representation labels and, for each $a\in I$, a finite-dimensional complex vector space $V_a$, a positive-definite Hermitian form $h_a$, and a smooth group homomorphism $\rho_a:G\to U(V_a,h_a)$. Here $U(V_a,h_a)$ is the group of complex-linear isometries of $h_a$, and a representation is the corresponding finite-dimensional group action. Its associated vector bundle is the quotient $E_a=P\times_{\rho_a}V_a$ with relation $[pg,v]=[p,\rho_a(g)v]$.

Two smooth right principal $G$-bundles over $M$ are isomorphic over $M$ when a smooth diffeomorphism between their total spaces covers $\operatorname{id}_M$ and commutes with the right $G$-actions. A **bundle sector** is one equivalence class under this relation. The datum specifies a set $\Sigma$ of admitted bundle sectors and requires $[P]\in\Sigma$; a model may take $\Sigma=\{[P]\}$. The Lie algebra alone does not replace the chosen group or sector. This definition does not choose a connection, an action functional, or a quantum theory.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, and let $\pi:P\to M$ be a smooth right principal $G$-bundle for a finite-dimensional real Lie group $G$, with $\mathfrak g=\operatorname{Lie}(G)=T_eG$. A supplied principal connection is a smooth, right-invariant complement $TP=VP\oplus H$, where $VP=\ker d\pi$; write $v:TP\to VP$ for the projection along $H$, and let $K_H(X,Y)=-v([hX,hY])$ be its vertical-valued curvature. For $Z\in\mathfrak g$ and $p\in P$, define the fundamental vertical vector $Z_P(p)=\left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_{t=0}p\exp_G(tZ)$. The orbit differential $\zeta_p: \mathfrak g\to V_pP$, $Z\mapsto Z_P(p)$, is a linear isomorphism, as proved below. Define the **principal connection 1-form** by

$$\omega_p(X):=\zeta_p^{-1}(v_pX),\qquad X\in T_pP.$$

Then $\omega$ is a smooth $\mathfrak g$-valued 1-form satisfying $\omega(Z_P)=Z$, $\ker\omega=H$, and $R_g^*\omega=\operatorname{Ad}_{g^{-1}}\omega$ for every fixed $g\in G$. Conversely, a smooth $\mathfrak g$-valued 1-form with the reproduction and equivariance properties determines the principal connection $H=\ker\omega$. The converted vertical curvature $\kappa_H:=\omega\circ K_H$ is a $\mathfrak g$-valued alternating 2-form; its equality with the Cartan curvature is established in the curvature lemma.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $M$ be a finite-dimensional smooth manifold, $G$ a finite-dimensional real Lie group, $\pi:P\to M$ a smooth right principal $G$-bundle, and $\omega$ the principal connection 1-form of a supplied horizontal distribution. Fix a finite-dimensional complex representation $\rho:G\to\operatorname{GL}_{\mathbb C}(V)$ that is smooth, and let $E=P\times_\rho V$ be its associated vector bundle with relation $[pg,v]=[p,\rho(g)v]$. Define $\rho_*:=d\rho_e:\mathfrak g\to\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V)$, where the differential is taken after viewing $\rho$ as a smooth matrix-valued map. For any open cover with smooth local sections $s_i:U_i\to P$, write $A_i=s_i^*\omega$. A smooth section $\sigma$ of $E$ has unique local components $\psi_i:U_i\to V$ given by $\sigma(x)=[s_i(x),\psi_i(x)]$. Define the **associated covariant derivative** $\nabla^\omega\sigma$ by its local components

$$
(\nabla^\omega\sigma)_i=d\psi_i+\rho_*(A_i)\psi_i,
$$

where $(\rho_*(A_i)\psi_i)(X)=\rho_*(A_i(X))\psi_i$ for $X\in TU_i$. These expressions patch to a smooth $E$-valued 1-form on $M$, independently of the chosen local sections, and satisfy $\nabla^\omega(f\sigma)=df\otimes\sigma+f\nabla^\omega\sigma$ for every smooth scalar function $f$ on $M$.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold and $\mathfrak g$ a finite-dimensional real Lie algebra. For homogeneous $\alpha\in\Omega^p(M,\mathfrak g)$ and $\beta\in\Omega^q(M,\mathfrak g)$, define their **graded bracket** by

$$[\alpha\wedge\beta](X_1,\ldots,X_{p+q}) := \frac{1}{p!q!}\sum_{\sigma\in S_{p+q}}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)[\alpha(X_{\sigma(1)},\ldots,X_{\sigma(p)}),\beta(X_{\sigma(p+1)},\ldots,X_{\sigma(p+q)})].$$

Here $\Omega^p(M,\mathfrak g)$ is the space of smooth alternating $p$-linear forms with values in $\mathfrak g$, the inner bracket is the Lie-algebra bracket, and the sum is over all permutations. This is a smooth $\mathfrak g$-valued $(p+q)$-form. It obeys graded skew-symmetry $[\alpha\wedge\beta]=-(-1)^{pq}[\beta\wedge\alpha]$, graded Jacobi

$$\left[\alpha\wedge\left[\beta\wedge\gamma\right]\right]=\left[\left[\alpha\wedge\beta\right]\wedge\gamma\right]+(-1)^{pq}\left[\beta\wedge\left[\alpha\wedge\gamma\right]\right],$$

and the exterior-derivative rule

$$d[\alpha\wedge\beta]=[d\alpha\wedge\beta]+(-1)^p[\alpha\wedge d\beta].$$

In particular, for $\mathfrak g$-valued 1-forms $A,B$, $[A\wedge B](X,Y)=[A(X),B(Y)]-[A(Y),B(X)]$, so $\tfrac12[A\wedge A](X,Y)=[A(X),A(Y)]$. This fixes the normalization used by the Cartan curvature formula.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, and let $\pi:P\to M$ be a smooth right principal $G$-bundle with a principal connection form $\omega$ associated to $H$, using $Z_P(p)=\left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_0p\exp_G(tZ)$ for the right action. For Lie-algebra-valued forms use the graded bracket defined by alternating shuffle and the Lie bracket; in degree one, $[A\wedge B](X,Y)=[A(X),B(Y)]-[A(Y),B(X)]$. Define

$$\Omega_\omega:=d\omega+\frac12[\omega\wedge\omega],\qquad D_\omega\eta:=d\eta+[\omega\wedge\eta].$$

Then $\Omega_\omega$ is horizontal and $\operatorname{Ad}$-equivariant, and $\Omega_\omega=\omega\circ K_H$ for the imported vertical-valued curvature $K_H(X,Y)=-v([hX,hY])$. For any trivializing cover with smooth sections $s_i:U_i\to P$, set $A_i=s_i^*\omega$ and $F_i=s_i^*\Omega_\omega$. On an overlap, let $g_{ij}:U_i\cap U_j\to G$ be the smooth map determined by $s_j=s_i g_{ij}$, and write $\theta_L(g_{ij})=g_{ij}^*\theta_L$ for the left Maurer–Cartan form. Then

$$A_j=\operatorname{Ad}_{g_{ij}^{-1}}A_i+\theta_L(g_{ij}),\qquad F_i=dA_i+\frac12[A_i\wedge A_i],\qquad F_j=\operatorname{Ad}_{g_{ij}^{-1}}F_i,\qquad D_{A_i}F_i=0,$$

where $D_{A_i}\eta:=d\eta+[A_i\wedge\eta]$. The transition equations concern changes of local sections; they do not identify an arbitrary map $M\to G$ with a global automorphism of a nontrivial bundle.

Let $G$ be either a real matrix Lie group $G\subseteq\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb R)$
with real Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$, or a complex matrix Lie group
$G\subseteq\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb C)$ with complex Lie algebra
$\mathfrak g$. In the real case let $K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$
and use polynomials in real linear coordinates with coefficients in $K$.
In the complex case take $K=\mathbb C$ and use polynomials in complex
linear coordinates (with no conjugate-coordinate variables). A homogeneous
degree-$k$ polynomial $P:\mathfrak g\to K$ is **$G$-invariant**
when
$$P(\operatorname{Ad}_g A)=P(A)\quad(g\in G,\ A\in\mathfrak g),$$
where the adjoint action is the one in
[[def-conjugation-and-the-adjoint-representation-of-a-lie-group]]. For
$k\geq1$, its polarization is the unique symmetric multilinear map
$P_k:\mathfrak g^k\to K$ with
$$P(A)=P_k(A,\ldots,A).$$
Here multilinearity is over $\mathbb R$ when $\mathfrak g$ is a real Lie
algebra and over $\mathbb C$ when it is a complex Lie algebra; thus a
$\mathbb C$-valued polynomial on a real Lie algebra still has a real-multilinear
polarization. A complex matrix Lie group may also be regarded as a real Lie
group, in which case the underlying real Lie algebra and real-multilinear
convention apply; this is also the convention for real-valued coordinate
polynomials on a complex matrix Lie algebra, such as $z\mapsto\operatorname{Re}z$
on $\mathfrak{gl}_1(\mathbb C)$.

The polarization can be computed by
$$P_k(A_1,\ldots,A_k)=\frac1{k!}[t_1\cdots t_k]P(t_1A_1+\cdots+t_kA_k),$$
where the bracket extracts the coefficient of $t_1\cdots t_k$. A homogeneous
degree-$k$ coordinate polynomial makes this coefficient symmetric and
multilinear in the $A_j$; setting every $A_j=A$ gives the coefficient
$k!P(A)$, and the same extraction proves uniqueness. Since $K$ has
characteristic zero, division by $k!$ is valid. For $k=0$, the invariant
polynomials are constants, viewed as symmetric $0$-linear forms $P_0\in K$.
Finite sums of these homogeneous invariant polynomials form the invariant
polynomial algebra; sums and products remain invariant because the adjoint
action respects addition and multiplication of scalar values.

Polarization preserves invariance: simultaneous application of $\operatorname{Ad}_g$
to the arguments leaves every term in the coefficient formula unchanged.
Conversely, if a symmetric $P_k$ is invariant under simultaneous adjoint action,
its diagonal $A\mapsto P_k(A,\ldots,A)$ is a $G$-invariant polynomial.
Differentiating that multilinear invariance along $g(t)=\exp(tX)$ gives the
infinitesimal identity
$$\sum_{j=1}^kP_k(A_1,\ldots,[X,A_j],\ldots,A_k)=0\quad(X\in\mathfrak g).$$
Indeed, for matrices,
$\left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_{0}\operatorname{Ad}_{\exp(tX)}A_j=[X,A_j]$,
so the chain rule gives exactly the displayed sum. For $k=0$ the sum is empty
and equals zero.

For $\mathfrak{gl}_r(\mathbb C)$, every coefficient of
$\det(I-tA)$ is invariant under $\operatorname{GL}_r(\mathbb C)$, since
$I-t(gAg^{-1})=g(I-tA)g^{-1}$ and determinant is unchanged by conjugation.
Its restriction to $\mathfrak u(r)$ is therefore invariant for the adjoint
action of $U(r)$. For the Pfaffian, use only
$\mathfrak{so}(2m)$ with $G=SO(2m)$ and a fixed oriented orthonormal frame.
For $A=(a_{ij})\in\mathfrak{so}(2m)$, define $\alpha_A=\frac12\sum_{i,j}
a_{ij}e^i\wedge e^j$ and set
$$\frac{\alpha_A^m}{m!}=\operatorname{Pf}(A)\,e^1\wedge\cdots\wedge e^{2m}.$$
This is a homogeneous polynomial of degree $m$. If $S\in O(2m)$, the induced
action on the top exterior power multiplies the oriented volume by $\det S$;
hence $\operatorname{Pf}(SAS^{\mathsf T})=(\det S)\operatorname{Pf}(A)$.
It is invariant under $SO(2m)$, and a reversal of orientation changes its
sign. The convention gives $\operatorname{Pf}\!\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&a\\-a&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)=a$; for $m=0$ it gives the empty-matrix Pfaffian $1$.

Let $M$ be a finite-dimensional Hausdorff second-countable smooth manifold,
possibly with boundary. Let $\mathbb F,\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$,
let $G$ be a real or complex matrix Lie group in
$\operatorname{GL}_r(\mathbb F)$, and let $\mathfrak g$ be its Lie algebra.
For a smooth rank-$r$ $\mathbb F$-vector bundle $E\to M$, a **$G$-frame
atlas** is a supplied open cover with local frames $e_\alpha$ whose transition
matrices $A_{\beta\alpha}$, defined by $e_\beta=e_\alpha A_{\beta\alpha}$,
take values in $G$. This is the local-frame description of a reduction of
the frame group to $G$. If $\mathbb F=\mathbb C$, a connection means a
complex connection as in
[[def-complex-linear-and-compatible-bundle-connections]]; for
$\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ it means an ordinary smooth bundle connection. A
connection is **compatible with this reduction** when its connection matrix
$\omega_\alpha$ in every supplied $G$-frame is $\mathfrak g$-valued. In
the convention of
[[thm-curvature-two-form-structure-equation]], its curvature matrix is
$$
\Omega_\alpha=d\omega_\alpha+\omega_\alpha\wedge\omega_\alpha.
$$
It is $\mathfrak g$-valued: for tangent vectors $X,Y$, the second term
evaluates to $[\omega_\alpha(X),\omega_\alpha(Y)]$, and both this bracket
and $d\omega_\alpha(X,Y)$ lie in $\mathfrak g$.

Let $P:\mathfrak g\to\mathbb K$ be a homogeneous degree-$k$
$G$-invariant polynomial, with symmetric multilinear polarization
$P_k$ as in [[def-invariant-polynomial-on-a-matrix-lie-algebra]]. For
$k\ge1$, define its **evaluation on curvature** in a supplied $G$-frame by
the alternating $2k$-form
$$
P_k(\Omega_\alpha,\ldots,\Omega_\alpha) =\sum_{a_1,\ldots,a_k} P_k(T_{a_1},\ldots,T_{a_k})\, \Omega_\alpha^{a_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge\Omega_\alpha^{a_k},
$$
where $(T_a)$ is any basis of $\mathfrak g$ and
$\Omega_\alpha=\sum_a T_a\otimes\Omega_\alpha^a$. The right side is the
multilinear extension of $P_k$ followed by exterior multiplication, so it is
independent of the chosen basis or tensor decomposition. Equivalently, for
$v_1,\ldots,v_{2k}\in T_xM$,
$$
\bigl(P_k(\Omega_\alpha^k)\bigr)_x(v_1,\ldots,v_{2k}) =\frac{1}{(2!)^k} \sum_{\sigma\in S_{2k}}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\, P_k\!\left( \Omega_\alpha(v_{\sigma(1)},v_{\sigma(2)}),\ldots, \Omega_\alpha(v_{\sigma(2k-1)},v_{\sigma(2k)}) \right).
$$
For $k=0$, set $P_0(\Omega_\alpha^0)=P_0$, the corresponding constant
$\mathbb K$-valued $0$-form. A finite sum of homogeneous invariant
polynomials is evaluated degree by degree and the resulting forms are added.

These local forms agree on overlaps. Indeed, [[prop-vector-bundle-curvature-is-an-endomorphism-valued-two-form]]
makes the curvature a global $\operatorname{End}(E)$-valued $2$-form. To
see its frame transformation, if a fibre vector has coordinate columns
$x_\alpha=A_{\beta\alpha}x_\beta$ and an endomorphism has matrices
$T_\alpha,T_\beta$, then $T_\beta=A_{\beta\alpha}^{-1}T_\alpha
A_{\beta\alpha}$. Applying this pointwise to curvature gives
$\Omega_\beta=A_{\beta\alpha}^{-1}\Omega_\alpha
A_{\beta\alpha}$. Since $A_{\beta\alpha}\in G$, simultaneous
$G$-invariance of $P_k$ gives
$$
P_k(\Omega_\beta,\ldots,\Omega_\beta) =P_k(\Omega_\alpha,\ldots,\Omega_\alpha).
$$
Thus the local evaluations define a global $\mathbb K$-valued $2k$-form.
For $\mathbb K=\mathbb C$, this means a complex-valued form, obtained by
complexifying the real form convention; the same local formulas are smooth up
to boundary charts by
[[lem-the-de-rham-complex-and-pullback-extend-to-manifolds-with-boundary]].

Let $M$ be a finite-dimensional Hausdorff second-countable smooth manifold,
possibly with boundary. Let $E\to M$ be a smooth rank-$r$ real or complex
vector bundle with a supplied $G$-frame atlas, where $G$ is a real or complex
matrix Lie group, and let $\nabla$ be a fixed connection compatible with that
reduction. For the algebra of finite sums of $\operatorname{Ad}(G)$-invariant
polynomials $P=\sum_k P_k$ with values in $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.
For each $P_k$, write $P_k^{\mathrm{pol}}$ for its normalized symmetric
polarization (with $P_0^{\mathrm{pol}}=P_0$), and define
$$\operatorname{CW}_{E,\nabla}(P)=\sum_k [P_k^{\mathrm{pol}}(\Omega_\nabla,\ldots,\Omega_\nabla)]\in H^{\mathrm{even}}_{\mathrm{dR}}(M;\mathbb K).$$
where a degree-$k$ polynomial maps to cohomological degree $2k$. The map is a
graded unital $\mathbb K$-algebra homomorphism, with polynomial multiplication
on the source and wedge product on the target, and
$\operatorname{CW}_{E,\nabla}(1)=[1]$. The coefficient convention for
$H_{\mathrm{dR}}(M;\mathbb K)$ on boundary manifolds is specified below.
This definition depends on the fixed connection; independence of its
cohomology value is a later theorem.

Let $M$ and $N$ be finite-dimensional Hausdorff second-countable smooth
manifolds, with boundary allowed. Let $E\to M$ be a finite-rank real or
complex bundle with a supplied $G$-frame reduction, where the applicable
group is $\operatorname{GL}_r(\mathbb R)$, $\operatorname{GL}_r(\mathbb C)$,
$U(r)$, or $SO(r)$. For a finite sum $P$ of $G$-invariant polynomials, let
$\operatorname{CW}_{E,\nabla}(P)$ be the map defined in
[[def-the-chern-weil-homomorphism]] using a connection compatible with this
same reduction.

For any two compatible connections $\nabla_0,\nabla_1$ on $E$,
$$\operatorname{CW}_{E,\nabla_0}(P)=\operatorname{CW}_{E,\nabla_1}(P).$$
For every smooth map $f:N\to M$, equip $f^*E$ with its pulled-back
$G$-reduction and use the pullback connection $f^*\nabla$. Then
$$\operatorname{CW}_{f^*E,f^*\nabla}(P)=f^*\operatorname{CW}_{E,\nabla}(P),$$
where for boundary manifolds smoothness and pullback of forms use the library's
local-extension convention. For each supplied compatible connection,
$\operatorname{CW}_{E,\nabla}$ is a unital graded algebra homomorphism in
$P$.

Assume full Axiom of Choice (AC) for the existence assertion: every such
real or complex bundle with a fixed $\operatorname{GL}$, $U$, or $SO$
reduction admits a compatible connection. The connection-independence and
pullback assertions for supplied compatible connections do not use AC.

Let $M$ be a finite-dimensional Hausdorff second-countable smooth manifold,
possibly with boundary. If $E\to M$ is a rank-$r$ complex vector bundle with
complex connection $\nabla$ and curvature $\Omega$, define the total Chern form
$$c(\nabla)=\det\!\left(I-\frac{\Omega}{2\pi i}\right)=\sum_{j=0}^r c_j(\nabla),$$
where $c_j(\nabla)$ has degree $2j$. For a Hermitian connection these forms
are real-valued; a general complex connection need not give real-valued forms.

For a rank-$r$ real vector bundle with real connection $\nabla$, let
$E_{\mathbb C}=E\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb C$ carry the complexified
connection $\nabla_{\mathbb C}$ and set
$$p_j(\nabla)=(-1)^j c_{2j}(\nabla_{\mathbb C})\quad\text{in degree }4j,\qquad p(\nabla)=\sum_{j\geq0}p_j(\nabla).$$
Then $p_0=1$, $p_j=0$ when $2j>r$, and every $p_j(\nabla)$ is real-valued,
even if $\nabla$ is not metric-compatible. If $\nabla$ is compatible with a
Euclidean metric, each odd Chern form $c_{2j+1}(\nabla_{\mathbb C})$ vanishes
pointwise. Assume full Axiom of Choice (AC); for every real connection each
$c_{2j+1}(\nabla_{\mathbb C})$ is then exact, with AC used through existence
of a metric-compatible connection and the transgression lemma.

If $E$ is an oriented Euclidean bundle of even rank $2m$ and $\nabla$ is
metric-compatible, define
$$e(\nabla)=\operatorname{Pf}\!\left(\frac{\Omega}{2\pi}\right),$$
where the Pfaffian uses the ordered oriented orthonormal frame and
$\operatorname{Pf}\!\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&a\\-a&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)=a$.
These curvature evaluations are closed forms. In rank zero,
$c(\nabla)=p(\nabla)=e(\nabla)=1$. The Euler form is defined here only for
oriented even-rank Euclidean bundles with a metric-compatible connection.

Assume full Axiom of Choice. Let $M$ be a finite-dimensional Hausdorff
second-countable smooth manifold, possibly with boundary or empty, and let
$\rho_M:H^*(M;\mathbb Z)\to H^*(M;\mathbb R)$ be induced by
$\mathbb Z\hookrightarrow\mathbb R$. Write $J_M$ for the natural de Rham
isomorphism from real de Rham cohomology to singular cohomology with real
coefficients.

For every finite-rank smooth complex bundle $E\to M$ with a Hermitian metric
and Hermitian connection $\nabla$, and every $j\geq0$,
$$J_M([c_j(\nabla)])=\rho_M(c_j(E)).$$
For every finite-rank smooth real bundle $V\to M$ with any real connection
$D$, and every $j\geq0$,
$$J_M([p_j(D)])=\rho_M(p_j(V)).$$
For every oriented Euclidean bundle $W\to M$ of even rank with a
metric-compatible connection $\nabla$, and its Thom-normalized Euler class,
$$J_M([e(\nabla)])=\rho_M(e(W)).$$
Here $c_j(\nabla)$, $p_j(D)$, and $e(\nabla)$ use the normalizations in
[[def-chern-pontryagin-and-euler-characteristic-forms]], while $c_j(E)$,
$p_j(V)$, and $e(W)$ are the published topological classes. In particular
$c_1(L)=e(L_{\mathbb R})$ for a complex line and
$p_j(V)=(-1)^j c_{2j}(V_{\mathbb C})$. These are equalities after passage to
real coefficients; no equality with integral torsion is asserted.

Assume AC. Let $E\to B$ be a numerable complex rank-$n$ bundle with $n\geq1$
over a path-connected CW complex $B$ (or over one of the CW-type bases of
[[thm-integral-complex-projective-bundle-theorem]]). By that theorem there are
unique classes $a_i\in H^{2i}(B;\mathbb Z)$, $1\leq i\leq n$, such that
$$x_E^{\,n}-a_1x_E^{\,n-1}+a_2x_E^{\,n-2}-\cdots+(-1)^na_n=0\qquad\text{in }H^{2n}(P(E);\mathbb Z),$$
where $x_E\in H^2(P(E);\mathbb Z)$ is the Euler class of the underlying real
bundle of the tautological line
([[def-complex-projective-bundle-and-tautological-complex-line]]). The
**Chern classes** of $E$ are these coefficients:
$$c_i(E):=a_i\in H^{2i}(B;\mathbb Z)\qquad(1\leq i\leq n),$$
completed by the conventions $c_0(E):=1\in H^0(B;\mathbb Z)$ and
$c_i(E):=0$ for $i>n$, and the **total Chern class** is the finite sum
$c(E):=\sum_{i\geq0}c_i(E)=1+c_1(E)+\cdots+c_n(E)\in H^*(B;\mathbb Z)$.

For the zero bundle of rank $0$ the conventions give $c(0_B)=1$. The definition
depends only on the isomorphism class of $E$, because an isomorphism of
bundles induces an isomorphism of projective bundles pulling $x$ back to $x$
and hence preserves the unique relation. For a complex line bundle $L\to B$ one
has $P(L)\cong B$ over $B$ with $\gamma_L$ corresponding to $L$ under that
identification, so the relation is $x_L-c_1(L)=0$; since $x_L=e(L_{\mathbb R})$
under the identification, this gives
$$c_1(L)=e(L_{\mathbb R}).$$
This is the normalization used throughout the page: the first Chern class of a
complex line is the Euler class of its underlying real bundle in the complex
orientation, not a separately chosen normalization.

Let $E\to M$ be a smooth real vector bundle of rank $2r$, where $r\geq0$,
over a smooth manifold that may have boundary. A **smooth complex structure**
on $E$ is a smooth bundle endomorphism $J:E\to E$ with $J^2=-I$. It makes
each fiber a complex vector space by $(a+ib)v=av+bJv$. Equivalently, $E$ has
local smooth complex frames with transition maps in $\operatorname{GL}_r(\mathbb C)$. In one direction, multiplication by $i$ in complex bundle charts gives
such a smooth $J$ because the transition maps are complex-linear. Conversely,
near any point choose a complex basis in its fiber and extend its vectors to
local smooth real sections; those sections together with their $J$-images
remain a real frame after shrinking the neighborhood, and give a local complex
frame. Forgetting smoothness in these charts gives the associated rank-$r$
complex topological vector bundle of
[[def-real-and-complex-topological-vector-bundle]].

For a smooth complex bundle $(E,J)$, write $\Gamma_{\mathbb C}(E)$ for its
smooth complex sections. A **complex connection** is a covariant derivative
$\nabla:\Gamma_{\mathbb C}(E)\to\Omega^1(M;E)$ that is $\mathbb C$-linear
and satisfies
$$\nabla(fs)=df\otimes s+f\nabla s$$
for every smooth complex-valued function $f$ and section $s$. This extends the
real bundle-connection convention of
[[def-connection-on-a-smooth-vector-bundle]]. A complex connection is
**Hermitian** for a supplied Hermitian metric $h$, taken linear in its first
variable and conjugate-linear in its second, when
$$Xh(s,t)=h(\nabla_Xs,t)+h(s,\nabla_Xt)$$
for all smooth sections $s,t$ and vector fields $X$. A real connection on a
Euclidean vector bundle is **Euclidean-compatible** when it obeys the same
identity for the real bundle metric, as in
[[def-metric-compatible-connection-on-a-riemannian-vector-bundle]].

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For every finite-dimensional Hausdorff second-countable smooth manifold $M$, possibly with boundary, integration on smooth simplices followed by the inverse of restriction from continuous to smooth singular cohomology gives a natural isomorphism of unital graded real algebras
$$J_M:H^*_{\mathrm{dR}}(M)\xrightarrow{\cong}H^*_{\mathrm{sing}}(M;\mathbb R).$$
The source product is wedge of form classes, the target product is the front/back singular cup product, and both stars denote direct sums of the homogeneous groups. Naturality is for smooth maps. No compactness assumption is imposed.

Let $V$ be a four-dimensional real vector space with an orientation and inner product $g$, and let $W$ be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space. Define the Hodge operator $*_g$ on $\Lambda^2V^*$ by $\alpha\wedge *_g\beta=\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_g\,\mathrm{vol}_g$, and extend it $W$-linearly to $\Lambda^2V^*\otimes W$. Give this tensor product the inner product induced by those on $\Lambda^2V^*$ and $W$. Then $*_g^2=I$, $*_g$ is an isometry, and its $+1$ and $-1$ eigenspaces are orthogonal. Every $\Phi\in\Lambda^2V^*\otimes W$ has the unique decomposition

$$
\Phi=\Phi^++\Phi^-,\qquad \Phi^\pm:=\frac{\Phi\pm *_g\Phi}{2},\qquad *_g\Phi^\pm=\pm\Phi^\pm.
$$

If the inner product on $V$ is rescaled to $\widehat g=\lambda^2g$ for any $\lambda>0$, then the Hodge operator on two-forms is unchanged: $*_{\widehat g}=*_g$.

derivations.claim: On an overlap with $s_j=s_i g_{ij}$, [F3] gives $F_j=\operatorname{Ad}_{g_{ij}^{-1}}F_i$. Since $B$ is invariant, $B(F_j\wedge F_j)=B(F_i\wedge F_i)$; these restrictions therefore define the global four-form $\beta_B$. The polynomial $P_B(Z)=B(Z,Z)/(8\pi^2)$ is homogeneous, quadratic, and $G$-invariant, so its curvature evaluation [F4] is exactly $\beta_B$. Connection independence of its Chern–Weil class follows from the supplied-connection clause of [F4].

For any two supplied connections on the same $G$-reduction, [F4] makes their Chern–Weil classes equal, so integration over the fixed orientation class gives the same $q_B$. In the $SU(2)$ defining representation, the associated connection matrix is $A_i$ because $\rho_*$ is the identity inclusion, and its curvature matrix is $\Omega_i=F_i$ by [F2, F3]. Put $C=i\Omega_i/(2\pi)=-\Omega_i/(2\pi i)$. Its entries have even form degree and commute, so the degree-four coefficient of $\det(I+C)$ is $\det C=\tfrac12((\operatorname{tr}_2C)^2-\operatorname{tr}_2(C\wedge C))$. By [F5], $\operatorname{tr}_2C=0$, and $C\wedge C=-\Omega_i\wedge\Omega_i/(4\pi^2)$; hence $c_2(\nabla)=\operatorname{tr}_2(\Omega_i\wedge\Omega_i)/(8\pi^2)$ and $\beta_B=-c_2(\nabla)$ because $B=-\operatorname{tr}_2$. The associated connection is Hermitian by [F7], so [F6] sends this de Rham class to the negative realification of $c_2(E)\in H^4(X;\mathbb Z)$. Evaluating by [F8] on the orientation class gives $q_B=-\langle c_2(E),[X]\rangle\in\mathbb Z$. Full AC is used only through the stated characteristic-class comparison and integral-class construction.

By [F9], $F_i^\pm=(F_i\pm *_gF_i)/2$ are the projections to the $\pm1$ eigenspaces, so $F_i^-=0$ is equivalent to $F_i=*_gF_i$, and $F_i^+=0$ is equivalent to $F_i=-*_gF_i$. The curvature transforms by the adjoint action on overlaps by [F3], while $*_g$ acts only on the form arguments, so each $F_i^\pm$ transforms by that same adjoint action. Thus $F^\pm$ are global adjoint-valued two-forms and the stated self-dual and ASD conditions do not depend on the local sections.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume full Axiom of Choice. Let $X$ be a nonempty, connected, compact, oriented, finite-dimensional Hausdorff second-countable smooth four-manifold without boundary, with a supplied Riemannian metric. Let $G\subseteq U(V,h)$ be a compact non-Abelian matrix Lie group in its specified global form, let $\pi:P\to X$ be a smooth right principal $G$-bundle in a specified bundle sector (an isomorphism class of smooth principal bundles under isomorphisms over $X$), and let $\omega$ be a supplied smooth principal connection. Let $B:\mathfrak g\times\mathfrak g\to\mathbb R$ be a positive-definite symmetric bilinear form invariant under $\operatorname{Ad}(G)$. For local sections $s_i:U_i\to P$, set $A_i=s_i^*\omega$ and $F_i=dA_i+\tfrac12[A_i\wedge A_i]$. If $F_i=\sum_a e_a F_i^a$ in a finite basis of $\mathfrak g$, define $B(F_i\wedge F_i):=\sum_{a,b}B(e_a,e_b)F_i^a\wedge F_i^b$; this expression is independent of the basis. Invariance of $B$ makes the local expressions $\beta_B|_{U_i}:=(8\pi^2)^{-1}B(F_i\wedge F_i)$ restrictions of a global four-form $\beta_B$. The **trace-normalized topological charge** is

$$
q_B(P,\omega):=\int_X\beta_B.
$$

The number $q_B(P,\omega)$ is independent of the supplied connection. For a general compact matrix group and invariant $B$, it is a real characteristic number; no integrality is asserted. In the special case $G=SU(2)$ in its defining representation on $\mathbb C^2$, with $h(v,w)=v^*w$ and $B(X,Y)=-\operatorname{tr}_2(XY)$, the associated Hermitian bundle $E=P\times_{SU(2)}\mathbb C^2$ has

$$
q_B(P,\omega)=-\langle c_2(E),[X]\rangle\in\mathbb Z,
$$

where $c_2(E)\in H^4(X;\mathbb Z)$ is the integral second Chern class and $[X]\in H_4(X;\mathbb Z)$ is the orientation fundamental class. This sign is fixed by the library convention $c(E,\nabla)=\det(I-\Omega_\nabla/(2\pi i))$.

The Hodge operator $*_g$ on two-forms is characterized by $\alpha\wedge *_g\beta=\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_g\,d\operatorname{vol}_g$ and acts componentwise on $\mathfrak g$-valued forms. Set $F_i^+=(F_i+*_gF_i)/2$ and $F_i^-=(F_i-*_gF_i)/2$. The self-dual sector consists of connections with $F_i^-=0$, equivalently $F_i=*_gF_i$; the anti-self-dual (ASD) sector consists of connections with $F_i^+=0$, equivalently $F_i=-*_gF_i$. These conditions are independent of the local section.

Assume full Axiom of Choice. Let $X$ be a nonempty, connected, compact, oriented, finite-dimensional Hausdorff second-countable smooth four-manifold without boundary, with a supplied Riemannian metric. Let $G\subseteq U(V,h)$ be a compact non-Abelian matrix Lie group in its specified global form, let $\pi:P\to X$ be a smooth right principal $G$-bundle in a specified bundle sector (an isomorphism class of smooth principal bundles under isomorphisms over $X$), and let $\omega$ be a supplied smooth principal connection. Let $B:\mathfrak g\times\mathfrak g\to\mathbb R$ be a positive-definite symmetric bilinear form invariant under $\operatorname{Ad}(G)$. For local sections $s_i:U_i\to P$, set $A_i=s_i^*\omega$ and $F_i=dA_i+\tfrac12[A_i\wedge A_i]$. If $F_i=\sum_a e_a F_i^a$ in a finite basis of $\mathfrak g$, define $B(F_i\wedge F_i):=\sum_{a,b}B(e_a,e_b)F_i^a\wedge F_i^b$; this expression is independent of the basis. Invariance of $B$ makes the local expressions $\beta_B|_{U_i}:=(8\pi^2)^{-1}B(F_i\wedge F_i)$ restrictions of a global four-form $\beta_B$. The **trace-normalized topological charge** is

$$

$$

The number $q_B(P,\omega)$ is independent of the supplied connection. For a general compact matrix group and invariant $B$, it is a real characteristic number; no integrality is asserted. In the special case $G=SU(2)$ in its defining representation on $\mathbb C^2$, with $h(v,w)=v^*w$ and $B(X,Y)=-\operatorname{tr}_2(XY)$, the associated Hermitian bundle $E=P\times_{SU(2)}\mathbb C^2$ has

$$
q_B(P,\omega)=-\langle c_2(E),[X]\rangle\in\mathbb Z,
$$

where $c_2(E)\in H^4(X;\mathbb Z)$ is the integral second Chern class and $[X]\in H_4(X;\mathbb Z)$ is the orientation fundamental class. This sign is fixed by the library convention $c(E,\nabla)=\det(I-\Omega_\nabla/(2\pi i))$.

The Hodge operator $*_g$ on two-forms is characterized by $\alpha\wedge *_g\beta=\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_g\,d\operatorname{vol}_g$ and acts componentwise on $\mathfrak g$-valued forms. Set $F_i^+=(F_i+*_gF_i)/2$ and $F_i^-=(F_i-*_gF_i)/2$. The self-dual sector consists of connections with $F_i^-=0$, equivalently $F_i=*_gF_i$; the anti-self-dual (ASD) sector consists of connections with $F_i^+=0$, equivalently $F_i=-*_gF_i$. These conditions are independent of the local section.

Let $V$ be a four-dimensional real vector space with an orientation and inner product $g$, and let $W$ be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space. Define the Hodge operator $*_g$ on $\Lambda^2V^*$ by $\alpha\wedge *_g\beta=\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_g\,\mathrm{vol}_g$, and extend it $W$-linearly to $\Lambda^2V^*\otimes W$. Give this tensor product the inner product induced by those on $\Lambda^2V^*$ and $W$. Then $*_g^2=I$, $*_g$ is an isometry, and its $+1$ and $-1$ eigenspaces are orthogonal. Every $\Phi\in\Lambda^2V^*\otimes W$ has the unique decomposition

$$
\Phi=\Phi^++\Phi^-,\qquad \Phi^\pm:=\frac{\Phi\pm *_g\Phi}{2},\qquad *_g\Phi^\pm=\pm\Phi^\pm.
$$

If the inner product on $V$ is rescaled to $\widehat g=\lambda^2g$ for any $\lambda>0$, then the Hodge operator on two-forms is unchanged: $*_{\widehat g}=*_g$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, and let $\pi:P\to M$ be a smooth right principal $G$-bundle with a principal connection form $\omega$ associated to $H$, using $Z_P(p)=\left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_0p\exp_G(tZ)$ for the right action. For Lie-algebra-valued forms use the graded bracket defined by alternating shuffle and the Lie bracket; in degree one, $[A\wedge B](X,Y)=[A(X),B(Y)]-[A(Y),B(X)]$. Define

$$\Omega_\omega:=d\omega+\frac12[\omega\wedge\omega],\qquad D_\omega\eta:=d\eta+[\omega\wedge\eta].$$

Then $\Omega_\omega$ is horizontal and $\operatorname{Ad}$-equivariant, and $\Omega_\omega=\omega\circ K_H$ for the imported vertical-valued curvature $K_H(X,Y)=-v([hX,hY])$. For any trivializing cover with smooth sections $s_i:U_i\to P$, set $A_i=s_i^*\omega$ and $F_i=s_i^*\Omega_\omega$. On an overlap, let $g_{ij}:U_i\cap U_j\to G$ be the smooth map determined by $s_j=s_i g_{ij}$, and write $\theta_L(g_{ij})=g_{ij}^*\theta_L$ for the left Maurer–Cartan form. Then

$$A_j=\operatorname{Ad}_{g_{ij}^{-1}}A_i+\theta_L(g_{ij}),\qquad F_i=dA_i+\frac12[A_i\wedge A_i],\qquad F_j=\operatorname{Ad}_{g_{ij}^{-1}}F_i,\qquad D_{A_i}F_i=0,$$

where $D_{A_i}\eta:=d\eta+[A_i\wedge\eta]$. The transition equations concern changes of local sections; they do not identify an arbitrary map $M\to G$ with a global automorphism of a nontrivial bundle.

derivations.claim: Write $F_i=F_i^++F_i^-$ with $*_{g_X}F_i^+=F_i^+$ and $*_{g_X}F_i^-=-F_i^-$. Let $a=\int_X B(F_i^+\wedge *_{g_X}F_i^+)$ and $b=\int_X B(F_i^-\wedge *_{g_X}F_i^-)$. Orthogonality of the two Hodge eigenspaces [F3] makes the cross terms vanish; positivity of $B$ [F2] gives $a,b\geq0$. Consequently $\int_XB(F_i\wedge *_{g_X}F_i)=a+b$, while $\int_XB(F_i\wedge F_i)=a-b$. By [F1], $S_B=(a+b)/g^2$ and $q_B=(a-b)/(8\pi^2)$.

For nonnegative $a,b$, $a+b\geq|a-b|$, so the claimed bound follows after division by $g^2>0$. If $q_B>0$, then $a>b$ and equality is equivalent to $b=0$. Its integrand is the continuous nonnegative squared norm of $F_i^-$; if $F_i^-$ were nonzero at a point, it would be bounded away from zero on a neighborhood of positive Riemannian volume, contradicting $b=0$. Thus $F_i^-=0$. If $q_B<0$, equality in $a+b\geq b-a$ is equivalent to $a=0$; the same continuity and positivity argument gives $F_i^+=0$. If $q_B=0$, equality forces $a+b=0$, so nonnegativity gives $a=b=0$ and both components vanish, hence $F_i=0$. Conversely each of the three stated conditions makes its corresponding norm vanish and gives equality.

By [F4], $D_{A_i}F_i=0$. For a self-dual connection, $D_{A_i}(*_{g_X}F_i)=D_{A_i}F_i=0$; for an anti-self-dual connection, $D_{A_i}(*_{g_X}F_i)=-D_{A_i}F_i=0$. This is the stated source-free Euclidean Yang–Mills equation. No boundary term or variational argument is used.

Assume full Axiom of Choice. Let $S^4=\{z\in\mathbb R^5:|z|=1\}$ have its unit round metric $g_X$. Denote by $p_\infty$ the point omitted by the north stereographic chart and by $p_0$ the point with north-chart coordinates $x=0$. Orient $S^4$ so that north-chart coordinates $x=(x^1,x^2,x^3,x^4)$ satisfy $dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3\wedge dx^4>0$. Set $r^2=\sum_{\mu=1}^4(x^\mu)^2$. The metric in the north chart is $4(1+r^2)^{-2}\sum_{\mu=1}^4(dx^\mu)^2$. Let $U_N=S^4\setminus\{p_\infty\}$ carry coordinate $x$, and $U_S=S^4\setminus\{p_0\}$ carry coordinate $y=x/r^2$; the metric in the south chart is $4(1+|y|^2)^{-2}\sum_{\mu=1}^4(dy^\mu)^2$.

Define $SU(2)=\{U\in M_2(\mathbb C):U^*U=I,\det U=1\}$. Write $\epsilon_{123}=1$ and let

$$ \sigma_1=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_3=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad T_a=-\frac{i}{2}\sigma_a. $$

The $T_a$ are traceless anti-Hermitian generators. Set $B(X,Y)=-\operatorname{tr}_2(XY)$. Define antisymmetric symbols by $\eta_{aij}=\epsilon_{aij}$, $\eta_{ai4}=\delta_{ai}$, $\bar\eta_{aij}=-\epsilon_{aij}$, and $\bar\eta_{ai4}=\delta_{ai}$ for spatial indices $i,j\in\{1,2,3\}$, where $\delta_{ai}$ is the Kronecker delta; extend them antisymmetrically in the last two indices. For a scale parameter $\rho>0$, define $u(x)=(x^4I-i x^j\sigma_j)/r\in SU(2)$ on $U_N\cap U_S$. Form the quotient of the two trivial right $SU(2)$-bundles by identifying $(x,h)_S\sim(x,u(x)^{-1}h)_N$ for each $x\in U_N\cap U_S$ and $h\in SU(2)$, so its local sections satisfy $s_S=s_Nu^{-1}$. Take the set of admitted bundle sectors to be the singleton containing the isomorphism class of this glued bundle, and take the representation family to be the singleton defining representation on $\mathbb C^2$. Define the local connection potentials by

$$ A_N=\frac{2\eta_{a\mu\nu}x^\nu}{r^2+\rho^2}T_a\,dx^\mu,\qquad A_S=-\frac{2\rho^2\bar\eta_{a\mu\nu}y^\nu}{1+\rho^2|y|^2}T_a\,dy^\mu. $$

On the overlap these obey $A_S=\operatorname{Ad}_u A_N+u\,d(u^{-1})$, so they define a smooth principal connection on the glued bundle. Let $F$ be its global curvature, with chart representatives $F_N$ and $F_S$. In the north chart its curvature, written $F_N=\tfrac12F^N_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu\wedge dx^\nu$, has components

$$ F^N_{\mu\nu}=-\frac{4\rho^2}{(r^2+\rho^2)^2}\eta_{a\mu\nu}T_a. $$

Let $*_{g_X}$ be the Hodge star characterized on two-forms by $\alpha\wedge *_{g_X}\beta=\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_{g_X}\,d\operatorname{vol}_X$, acting componentwise on the Lie-algebra coefficients. This curvature is self-dual, meaning $F_N=*_{g_X}F_N$. With $B$ as fixed above, define the charge by $q_B=(8\pi^2)^{-1}\int_{S^4}B(F\wedge F)$ and, for any real $g>0$, define the action by $S_B(g)=g^{-2}\int_{S^4}B(F\wedge *_{g_X}F)$. Then $q_B=1$, $S_B(g)=8\pi^2/g^2<\infty$, and the action saturates the self-dual bound. This is one explicit Belavin–Polyakov–Schwartz–Tyupkin (BPST) charge-one connection; no uniqueness or moduli classification is asserted.

derivations.claim: Apply [F1] with the given $\rho>0$ and $g>0$, round metric, north-chart orientation, Pauli matrices, transition $u^{-1}$ and trace form $B=-\operatorname{tr}_2$. These are exactly the hypotheses and explicit formulas of the proposition, so it applies to the displayed local data.
Its conclusions give every asserted property, including the global smooth connection, displayed curvature, self-duality, $q_B=1$ and $S_B(g)=8\pi^2/g^2$. No classification follows.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and let $n\geq1$. Regarded as real Lie groups,

$$U(n)=\{A\in\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb C):A^*A=I\},\qquad SU(n)=\{A\in U(n):\det A=1\}$$

have Lie algebras

$$\mathfrak u(n)=\{X:X^*+X=0\},\qquad \mathfrak{su}(n)=\{X\in\mathfrak u(n):\operatorname{tr}X=0\}.$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, and let $\pi:P\to M$ be a smooth right principal $G$-bundle for a finite-dimensional real Lie group $G$, with $\mathfrak g=\operatorname{Lie}(G)=T_eG$. A supplied principal connection is a smooth, right-invariant complement $TP=VP\oplus H$, where $VP=\ker d\pi$; write $v:TP\to VP$ for the projection along $H$, and let $K_H(X,Y)=-v([hX,hY])$ be its vertical-valued curvature. For $Z\in\mathfrak g$ and $p\in P$, define the fundamental vertical vector $Z_P(p)=\left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_{t=0}p\exp_G(tZ)$. The orbit differential $\zeta_p: \mathfrak g\to V_pP$, $Z\mapsto Z_P(p)$, is a linear isomorphism, as proved below. Define the **principal connection 1-form** by

$$\omega_p(X):=\zeta_p^{-1}(v_pX),\qquad X\in T_pP.$$

Then $\omega$ is a smooth $\mathfrak g$-valued 1-form satisfying $\omega(Z_P)=Z$, $\ker\omega=H$, and $R_g^*\omega=\operatorname{Ad}_{g^{-1}}\omega$ for every fixed $g\in G$. Conversely, a smooth $\mathfrak g$-valued 1-form with the reproduction and equivariance properties determines the principal connection $H=\ker\omega$. The converted vertical curvature $\kappa_H:=\omega\circ K_H$ is a $\mathfrak g$-valued alternating 2-form; its equality with the Cartan curvature is established in the curvature lemma.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, and let $\pi:P\to M$ be a smooth right principal $G$-bundle with a principal connection form $\omega$ associated to $H$, using $Z_P(p)=\left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_0p\exp_G(tZ)$ for the right action. For Lie-algebra-valued forms use the graded bracket defined by alternating shuffle and the Lie bracket; in degree one, $[A\wedge B](X,Y)=[A(X),B(Y)]-[A(Y),B(X)]$. Define

$$\Omega_\omega:=d\omega+\frac12[\omega\wedge\omega],\qquad D_\omega\eta:=d\eta+[\omega\wedge\eta].$$

Then $\Omega_\omega$ is horizontal and $\operatorname{Ad}$-equivariant, and $\Omega_\omega=\omega\circ K_H$ for the imported vertical-valued curvature $K_H(X,Y)=-v([hX,hY])$. For any trivializing cover with smooth sections $s_i:U_i\to P$, set $A_i=s_i^*\omega$ and $F_i=s_i^*\Omega_\omega$. On an overlap, let $g_{ij}:U_i\cap U_j\to G$ be the smooth map determined by $s_j=s_i g_{ij}$, and write $\theta_L(g_{ij})=g_{ij}^*\theta_L$ for the left Maurer–Cartan form. Then

$$A_j=\operatorname{Ad}_{g_{ij}^{-1}}A_i+\theta_L(g_{ij}),\qquad F_i=dA_i+\frac12[A_i\wedge A_i],\qquad F_j=\operatorname{Ad}_{g_{ij}^{-1}}F_i,\qquad D_{A_i}F_i=0,$$

where $D_{A_i}\eta:=d\eta+[A_i\wedge\eta]$. The transition equations concern changes of local sections; they do not identify an arbitrary map $M\to G$ with a global automorphism of a nontrivial bundle.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold and $\mathfrak g$ a finite-dimensional real Lie algebra. For homogeneous $\alpha\in\Omega^p(M,\mathfrak g)$ and $\beta\in\Omega^q(M,\mathfrak g)$, define their **graded bracket** by

$$[\alpha\wedge\beta](X_1,\ldots,X_{p+q}) := \frac{1}{p!q!}\sum_{\sigma\in S_{p+q}}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)[\alpha(X_{\sigma(1)},\ldots,X_{\sigma(p)}),\beta(X_{\sigma(p+1)},\ldots,X_{\sigma(p+q)})].$$

Here $\Omega^p(M,\mathfrak g)$ is the space of smooth alternating $p$-linear forms with values in $\mathfrak g$, the inner bracket is the Lie-algebra bracket, and the sum is over all permutations. This is a smooth $\mathfrak g$-valued $(p+q)$-form. It obeys graded skew-symmetry $[\alpha\wedge\beta]=-(-1)^{pq}[\beta\wedge\alpha]$, graded Jacobi

$$\left[\alpha\wedge\left[\beta\wedge\gamma\right]\right]=\left[\left[\alpha\wedge\beta\right]\wedge\gamma\right]+(-1)^{pq}\left[\beta\wedge\left[\alpha\wedge\gamma\right]\right],$$

and the exterior-derivative rule

$$d[\alpha\wedge\beta]=[d\alpha\wedge\beta]+(-1)^p[\alpha\wedge d\beta].$$

In particular, for $\mathfrak g$-valued 1-forms $A,B$, $[A\wedge B](X,Y)=[A(X),B(Y)]-[A(Y),B(X)]$, so $\tfrac12[A\wedge A](X,Y)=[A(X),A(Y)]$. This fixes the normalization used by the Cartan curvature formula.

Assume full Axiom of Choice. Let $X$ be a nonempty, connected, compact, oriented, finite-dimensional Hausdorff second-countable smooth four-manifold without boundary, with a supplied Riemannian metric. Let $G\subseteq U(V,h)$ be a compact non-Abelian matrix Lie group in its specified global form, let $\pi:P\to X$ be a smooth right principal $G$-bundle in a specified bundle sector (an isomorphism class of smooth principal bundles under isomorphisms over $X$), and let $\omega$ be a supplied smooth principal connection. Let $B:\mathfrak g\times\mathfrak g\to\mathbb R$ be a positive-definite symmetric bilinear form invariant under $\operatorname{Ad}(G)$. For local sections $s_i:U_i\to P$, set $A_i=s_i^*\omega$ and $F_i=dA_i+\tfrac12[A_i\wedge A_i]$. If $F_i=\sum_a e_a F_i^a$ in a finite basis of $\mathfrak g$, define $B(F_i\wedge F_i):=\sum_{a,b}B(e_a,e_b)F_i^a\wedge F_i^b$; this expression is independent of the basis. Invariance of $B$ makes the local expressions $\beta_B|_{U_i}:=(8\pi^2)^{-1}B(F_i\wedge F_i)$ restrictions of a global four-form $\beta_B$. The **trace-normalized topological charge** is

$$
q_B(P,\omega):=\int_X\beta_B.
$$

The number $q_B(P,\omega)$ is independent of the supplied connection. For a general compact matrix group and invariant $B$, it is a real characteristic number; no integrality is asserted. In the special case $G=SU(2)$ in its defining representation on $\mathbb C^2$, with $h(v,w)=v^*w$ and $B(X,Y)=-\operatorname{tr}_2(XY)$, the associated Hermitian bundle $E=P\times_{SU(2)}\mathbb C^2$ has

$$
q_B(P,\omega)=-\langle c_2(E),[X]\rangle\in\mathbb Z,
$$

where $c_2(E)\in H^4(X;\mathbb Z)$ is the integral second Chern class and $[X]\in H_4(X;\mathbb Z)$ is the orientation fundamental class. This sign is fixed by the library convention $c(E,\nabla)=\det(I-\Omega_\nabla/(2\pi i))$.

The Hodge operator $*_g$ on two-forms is characterized by $\alpha\wedge *_g\beta=\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_g\,d\operatorname{vol}_g$ and acts componentwise on $\mathfrak g$-valued forms. Set $F_i^+=(F_i+*_gF_i)/2$ and $F_i^-=(F_i-*_gF_i)/2$. The self-dual sector consists of connections with $F_i^-=0$, equivalently $F_i=*_gF_i$; the anti-self-dual (ASD) sector consists of connections with $F_i^+=0$, equivalently $F_i=-*_gF_i$. These conditions are independent of the local section.

Assume full Axiom of Choice. Let $X$ be a nonempty, connected, compact, oriented, finite-dimensional Hausdorff second-countable smooth four-manifold without boundary, with Riemannian metric $g_X$. Let $G\subseteq U(V,h)$ be a compact non-Abelian matrix Lie group in its specified global form, let $P\to X$ be a smooth right principal $G$-bundle, and let $\omega$ be a supplied smooth principal connection. Let $B$ be a positive-definite, symmetric, $\operatorname{Ad}(G)$-invariant bilinear form on $\mathfrak g$. For any local section $s_i$, set $A_i=s_i^*\omega$ and $F_i=dA_i+\tfrac12[A_i\wedge A_i]$. Invariance of $B$ makes the local four-forms $\beta_B|_{U_i}=\frac{1}{8\pi^2}B(F_i\wedge F_i)$ and $\gamma_B|_{U_i}=B(F_i\wedge *_{g_X}F_i)$ restrictions of global forms. Define $q_B=\int_X\beta_B$. For a real scalar $g>0$, define the Euclidean Yang–Mills functional by

$$
S_B(P,\omega):=\frac{1}{g^2}\int_X\gamma_B,
$$

where the Hodge operator is characterized by $\alpha\wedge *_{g_X}\beta=\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_{g_X}\,d\operatorname{vol}_{g_X}$ and acts componentwise on $\mathfrak g$-valued forms. Then

$$
S_B(P,\omega)\geq \frac{8\pi^2}{g^2}\,|q_B(P,\omega)|.
$$

Equality holds exactly in these cases: if $q_B>0$, then $F_i=*_{g_X}F_i$; if $q_B<0$, then $F_i=-*_{g_X}F_i$; if $q_B=0$, then $F_i=0$. Every self-dual or anti-self-dual supplied connection satisfies the source-free Euclidean Yang–Mills equation $D_{A_i}(*_{g_X}F_i)=0$, where $D_{A_i}\eta=d\eta+[A_i\wedge\eta]$. The statement asserts neither existence nor uniqueness of a connection in any charge sector.

Assume the axiom of countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $M$ be a finite-dimensional, Hausdorff, second-countable smooth manifold without boundary. A **non-Abelian gauge datum on $M$** consists of the following specified objects.

First choose a finite-dimensional real Lie group $G$ that is compact in its manifold topology (every open cover has a finite subcover) and noncommutative (there are $g,h\in G$ with $gh\ne hg$). The actual group $G$, including its global form, is part of the datum. Its Lie algebra is $\mathfrak g=\operatorname{Lie}(G)=T_eG$ with the bracket transported from left-invariant smooth vector fields.

Choose a smooth right principal $G$-bundle $\pi:P\to M$: the projection and right action are smooth, and the action is free and transitive on each fibre. There is an open cover $\{U_\alpha\}_{\alpha\in A}$ of $M$ with a family of equivariant diffeomorphisms $\phi_\alpha:\pi^{-1}(U_\alpha)\to U_\alpha\times G$ for $\alpha\in A$, each over $U_\alpha$. Explicitly, $\operatorname{pr}_1\circ\phi_\alpha=\pi$, and if $\phi_\alpha(p)=(x,g)$ then $\phi_\alpha(ph)=(x,gh)$ for every $h\in G$.

Choose a specified set $I$ of representation labels and, for each $a\in I$, a finite-dimensional complex vector space $V_a$, a positive-definite Hermitian form $h_a$, and a smooth group homomorphism $\rho_a:G\to U(V_a,h_a)$. Here $U(V_a,h_a)$ is the group of complex-linear isometries of $h_a$, and a representation is the corresponding finite-dimensional group action. Its associated vector bundle is the quotient $E_a=P\times_{\rho_a}V_a$ with relation $[pg,v]=[p,\rho_a(g)v]$.

Two smooth right principal $G$-bundles over $M$ are isomorphic over $M$ when a smooth diffeomorphism between their total spaces covers $\operatorname{id}_M$ and commutes with the right $G$-actions. A **bundle sector** is one equivalence class under this relation. The datum specifies a set $\Sigma$ of admitted bundle sectors and requires $[P]\in\Sigma$; a model may take $\Sigma=\{[P]\}$. The Lie algebra alone does not replace the chosen group or sector. This definition does not choose a connection, an action functional, or a quantum theory.

Let $X$ be a Hausdorff, second-countable smooth manifold covered by open sets $U$ and $V$. Let $G$ be a finite-dimensional, Hausdorff, second-countable real Lie group, and let $\tau:U\cap V\to G$ be smooth. On the disjoint union $Q=(U\times G)_U\sqcup(V\times G)_V$, impose the equivalence relation generated, for $x\in U\cap V$ and $h\in G$, by

$$ (x,h)_V\sim (x,\tau(x)h)_U. $$

Let $P:=Q/{\sim}$ with the quotient topology, write $[x,h]_U$ and $[x,h]_V$ for its classes, and define $\pi:P\to X$ by $\pi([x,h]_U)=\pi([x,h]_V)=x$. Define the right action by $[x,h]_i\cdot k=[x,hk]_i$ for $k\in G$ and $i\in\{U,V\}$. Then $P$ is a smooth right principal $G$-bundle over $X$. Its local sections $s_U(x)=[x,e]_U$ and $s_V(x)=[x,e]_V$ satisfy $s_V(x)=s_U(x)\tau(x)$ on $U\cap V$.

Let $V$ be a four-dimensional real vector space with an orientation and inner product $g$, and let $W$ be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space. Define the Hodge operator $*_g$ on $\Lambda^2V^*$ by $\alpha\wedge *_g\beta=\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_g\,\mathrm{vol}_g$, and extend it $W$-linearly to $\Lambda^2V^*\otimes W$. Give this tensor product the inner product induced by those on $\Lambda^2V^*$ and $W$. Then $*_g^2=I$, $*_g$ is an isometry, and its $+1$ and $-1$ eigenspaces are orthogonal. Every $\Phi\in\Lambda^2V^*\otimes W$ has the unique decomposition

$$
\Phi=\Phi^++\Phi^-,\qquad \Phi^\pm:=\frac{\Phi\pm *_g\Phi}{2},\qquad *_g\Phi^\pm=\pm\Phi^\pm.
$$

If the inner product on $V$ is rescaled to $\widehat g=\lambda^2g$ for any $\lambda>0$, then the Hodge operator on two-forms is unchanged: $*_{\widehat g}=*_g$.

Assume full AC. Give the unit sphere $S^4\subset\mathbb R^5$ its boundary orientation, round metric and standard spin structure induced from the Euclidean ball. Let $S=S^+\oplus S^-$ be its complex spinor bundle, with skew-Hermitian Clifford action $c(v)c(w)+c(w)c(v)=-2\langle v,w\rangle$ and positive chirality the $+1$ eigenspace of $\Gamma=-c(e_1)c(e_2)c(e_3)c(e_4)$ in an oriented orthonormal frame. A spin lift here is a principal $\operatorname{Spin}(4)$ bundle double-covering the oriented orthonormal frame bundle; explicitly $\operatorname{Spin}(4)=Sp(1)\times Sp(1)$ covers $SO(4)$ by $(a,b):q\mapsto aqb^{-1}$ on $\mathbb H\cong\mathbb R^4$, where $Sp(1)$ is the unit-quaternion group, identified with $SU(2)$. The connection on spinors is the lift of the Levi-Civita connection. Set $E=S^+$ with its rank-two Hermitian $SU(2)$ connection $A_+$.

For complex Banach spaces $X,Y$, a bounded complex-linear map $T:X\to Y$ is Fredholm when its range is closed and both $\ker T$ and $\operatorname{coker}T:=Y/\operatorname{ran}T$ are finite dimensional; its index is $\operatorname{ind}_{\mathbb C}T:=\dim_{\mathbb C}\ker T-\dim_{\mathbb C}\operatorname{coker}T$. Here $L^2$ uses the bundle metric and Riemannian volume, and $H^1$ is the completion of smooth sections in the norm $\|u\|_{H^1}^2=\|u\|_2^2+\|\nabla u\|_2^2$, equivalent to the finite-chart Sobolev norm. These are complex Hilbert, hence Banach, spaces. A smooth first-order differential operator on this compact base is bounded from $H^1$ to $L^2$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M,E,P$ have exactly the compact, boundaryless, scalar-positive-symbol and formal symmetry hypotheses of [[thm-elliptic-differential-operators-on-compact-vector-bundles-have-parametrices-and-regularity]], with $\operatorname{dom}P=H^2(M,E)$. Write $\mathcal H=\ker P$.

Then $\mathcal H$ is finite dimensional and consists of smooth sections, $\operatorname{ran}P=\mathcal H^\perp$ is closed in $L^2$, and
$$L^2(M,E)=\mathcal H\mathbin{\oplus^\perp}\operatorname{ran}P.$$
Let $\Pi$ be the orthogonal projection onto $\mathcal H$. There is a unique linear operator $G:L^2\to H^2\cap\mathcal H^\perp$ with
$$PG=I-\Pi\quad\hbox{on }L^2,\qquad GP=I-\Pi\quad\hbox{on }H^2,\qquad G\Pi=\Pi G=0.$$
It is bounded from $H^k$ to $H^{k+2}$ for every integer $k\ge0$, compact and selfadjoint on $L^2$, and preserves smooth sections. For all such $k$,
$$H^k=\mathcal H\oplus P(H^{k+2}),\qquad C^\infty(M,E)=\mathcal H\oplus P(C^\infty(M,E)),$$
where the second summands are the corresponding intersections with $\mathcal H^\perp$, and the decompositions are topological. The projection is smoothing: for every integer $r\ge0$, $\|\Pi f\|_{C^r}\le C_r\|f\|_2$. Consequently $G$ is a two-sided parametrix with finite-rank smoothing remainders. If additionally $(Pu,u)_2\ge0$ for smooth $u$, then $P$ and $G$ are nonnegative on their respective domains.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold without boundary of real dimension $n\ge2$, equipped with a smooth positive density, and $E\to M$ a finite-rank real Euclidean or complex Hermitian smooth vector bundle. Let $P$ be a smooth-coefficient second-order differential operator on $E$, formally symmetric for the density and metric, whose positive-frequency principal symbol is
$$\sigma_2(P)(x,\xi)=a_x(\xi,\xi)I_{E_x},$$
where $a$ is a smooth positive-definite real quadratic form on cotangent vectors. Thus in any local frame $P=-a^{ij}\partial_i\partial_j+B^j\partial_j+C$, with scalar real positive-definite $a^{ij}$ and matrix-valued lower coefficients. Nonnegativity of $P$ is not needed here.

For nonnegative integers $k$, define $H^k(M,E)$ by requiring the coefficients of each member of a finite smooth partition of unity times the section, in precompact bundle charts and extended by zero, to lie in $H^k(\mathbb R^n)$; the norm is the square root of the sum of these component Sobolev norms squared. Different such choices give equivalent norms. The following hold.

1. These are Hilbert spaces, smooth sections are dense, $H^0=L^2$ with equivalent norms, $H^{k+1}\hookrightarrow H^k$ is compact, and $H^k\hookrightarrow C^r$ continuously whenever $k>r+n/2$.
2. If $u\in H^1$ and $Pu=f\in H^k$ distributionally, then $u\in H^{k+2}$ and
$$\|u\|_{H^{k+2}}\le C_k(\|f\|_{H^k}+\|u\|_{L^2}).$$
In particular smooth data give smooth weak solutions. The same estimate holds for all $u\in H^{k+2}$.
3. For sufficiently large real $\lambda>0$, $P+\lambda:H^2\to L^2$ is a bounded bijection with bounded inverse $B:L^2\to H^2$. As an operator on $L^2$, $B$ is compact, injective and selfadjoint, has dense range $H^2$, and the unbounded operator $P$ with domain exactly $H^2$ is selfadjoint. $$PB=I-\lambda B\quad\hbox{on }L^2,\qquad BP=I-\lambda B\quad\hbox{on }H^2.$$
Here on the second space $B$ denotes its restriction after inclusion $H^2\hookrightarrow L^2$; it is compact on $H^2$. No assertion concerning arbitrary-order elliptic operators, or pseudodifferential symbol classes, is part of this theorem.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be Banach spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb F$
([[def-banach-space]]) and let $T:X\to Y$ be a bounded linear operator
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). Then $T$ is a **Fredholm operator** when
all three of the following hold:

1. $\ker T$ is finite dimensional, that is, admits an ordered basis of finite
   length ([[def-linear-basis]], [[def-dimension]]);
2. $\operatorname{ran}T$ is a closed subspace of $Y$
   ([[def-linear-subspace]]);
3. the **cokernel** $\operatorname{coker}T:=Y/\operatorname{ran}T$ is finite
   dimensional ([[def-quotient-vector-space-coset-notation]],
   [[def-dimension]]).

Here the cokernel is the algebraic quotient vector space; it also carries the
quotient seminorm of [[def-quotient-seminorm]], which is a norm when the range
is closed ([[thm-quotient-seminorm-is-a-norm-iff-subspace-is-closed]]), but the dimension in clause 3 is the vector-space dimension of the
quotient and does not depend on that norm.

For a Fredholm operator $T$ the **index** of $T$ is the integer

$$\operatorname{ind}T:=\dim_{\mathbb F}\ker T-\dim_{\mathbb F}\operatorname{coker}T$$

Here subtraction is in $\mathbb Z$, not in $\mathbb N$: write $a=\dim_{\mathbb F}\ker T$ and $b=\dim_{\mathbb F}\operatorname{coker}T$ and identify a natural $n$ with $[(n,0)]$. Precisely,

$$\operatorname{ind}T=[(a,b)]=[(a,0)]+(-[(b,0)])\in\mathbb Z$$

by [[def-integers]] and [[def-int-operations]]. Both dimensions are natural numbers, so this class is defined even when $a<b$; the index may be positive, negative or zero.

**Two remarks on the definition.** The closedness of the range is listed
explicitly as a hypothesis of the definition rather than extracted from the
other clauses. And no property of the index is asserted here; additivity,
local constancy and invariance under compact perturbations are separate
theorems.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: For any given spin four-manifold the local quaternionic model glues by its specified Spin(4) lift. In that quaternionic spin model, right multiplication by a quaternionic unit $j$ is an antiunitary map $J_0$ on $S^+\oplus S^-$, with $J_0^2=-1$. It commutes with the four Clifford matrices and $\Gamma$ and is parallel: the transition and connection matrices act from the left and hence commute with right multiplication. The same operation $J_E$ on the $SU(2)$ twist is parallel, antiunitary and has square $-1$. Define $J_5=\Gamma J_0$ on the spin factor. Then $J_5^2=-1$, it anticommutes with each of the four tangent Clifford matrices, and it anticommutes with $c_5=i\Gamma$ because anti-linearity changes $i$ to $-i$. Thus it is the pseudoreal Spin(5) structure, since even products of Clifford matrices commute with it. On the complex tensor product set $J=J_5\otimes J_E$; it is well-defined and antiunitary, $J^2=1$, and $JD_5=-D_5J$. Hence $J$ preserves the kernel and $iD_5$ commutes with $J$.

Chirality anticommutes with $D_4$ and is parallel, so $D_5^2=D_4^2-\partial_t^2$. It has scalar positive principal symbol and smooth coefficients. Formal symmetry follows from unitary connection compatibility and periodic integration by parts. The same shifted-resolvent argument applies to $D_4$ and $D_5$ on a general compact background: each square has scalar positive principal symbol, and [F2] gives the inverse of its positive shift from $L^2$ to $H^2$; multiplying by $D_j\mp i$ gives surjectivity of $D_j\pm i$ and the $H^1$ selfadjoint domain exactly as in [F1]. An $L^2$ weak chiral cokernel vector also has square zero distributionally; testing against smooth sections and using their $H^2$ density puts it in the adjoint domain of the selfadjoint square, hence in $H^2$, and [F2] then makes it smooth. Since [F3] gives closed range, orthogonal projection identifies its quotient cokernel with this smooth negative-chirality kernel. Weak kernels are smooth by the same argument. For a zero mode $\psi$, integration by parts gives $0=\|D_5\psi\|^2=\|D_4\psi\|^2+\|\partial_t\psi\|^2$. Thus $\psi$ is independent of $t$ and lies in $\ker D_4$; conversely every such spinor gives a periodic product zero mode. In general its complex dimension is $n_++n_-$, identifying the smooth negative-chirality kernel with the cokernel by the formal $L^2$ adjoint. For the concrete round twist this dimension is $1$ by [F1]. This avoids any unproved general spectral-flow identity.

The constant central automorphism acts by $-1$ on both chiral spinor kernels and cokernels, and fixes the background connection. Its scalar on the inverse determinant line is $(-1)^{-n_+}(-1)^{n_-}=(-1)^{n_+-n_-}$. For the actual round twist [F1] gives dimensions one and zero, hence scalar $-1$. Parallel transport along a constant path is the identity for any connection. Closing by the inverse endpoint identification gives $z_*^{-1}\circ\mathrm{PT}=-1$; tensor powers give $(-1)^N$. This is an actual finite-dimensional exterior-power action, not an assumption equating a periodic eta invariant with holonomy.

For any finite-dimensional complex vector space $V$ with anti-linear involution $J$, every $v$ has the unique decomposition $v=(v+Jv)/2+i(v-Jv)/(2i)$ with both displayed real components fixed by $J$. The restriction of $iD_5$ is real and skew-adjoint, because $D_5$ is selfadjoint and $J(iD_5)=(iD_5)J$. Its real kernel has dimension $n_++n_-$. This has the same parity as $n_+-n_-$, since their difference is $2n_-$. For the concrete round twist the real dimension and parity are one by [F1].

For antiperiodic boundary conditions the energy argument in step 1.2 would again force a zero mode to be constant in $t$, but a constant antiperiodic spinor is zero. In a mapping-torus clutch the total spinor boundary multiplier is the product of its spin and gauge multipliers. The central gauge multiplier is $-1$, so a bounding/antiperiodic spin multiplier $-1$ makes the total periodic, whereas a nonbounding/periodic spin multiplier $+1$ makes it antiperiodic. Moving the central sign from the gauge clutch to the spin clutch therefore exchanges these two spin conventions, exactly as stated.

$$ \sigma_1=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_3=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad T_a=-\frac{i}{2}\sigma_a. $$

The $T_a$ are traceless anti-Hermitian generators. Set $B(X,Y)=-\operatorname{tr}_2(XY)$. Define antisymmetric symbols by $\eta_{aij}=\epsilon_{aij}$, $\eta_{ai4}=\delta_{ai}$, $\bar\eta_{aij}=-\epsilon_{aij}$, and $\bar\eta_{ai4}=\delta_{ai}$ for spatial indices $i,j\in\{1,2,3\}$, where $\delta_{ai}$ is the Kronecker delta; extend them antisymmetrically in the last two indices. $$ A_N=\frac{2\eta_{a\mu\nu}x^\nu}{r^2+\rho^2}T_a\,dx^\mu,\qquad A_S=-\frac{2\rho^2\bar\eta_{a\mu\nu}y^\nu}{1+\rho^2|y|^2}T_a\,dy^\mu. $$

$$ F^N_{\mu\nu}=-\frac{4\rho^2}{(r^2+\rho^2)^2}\eta_{a\mu\nu}T_a. $$

Let $*_{g_X}$ be the Hodge star characterized on two-forms by $\alpha\wedge *_{g_X}\beta=\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_{g_X}\,d\operatorname{vol}_X$, acting componentwise on the Lie-algebra coefficients. This curvature is self-dual, meaning $F_N=*_{g_X}F_N$. $$
q_B(P,\omega):=\int_X\beta_B.

is closed ([[thm-quotient-seminorm-is-a-norm-iff-subspace-is-closed]]), but the dimension in clause 3 is the vector-space dimension of the
quotient and does not depend on that norm.

For a Fredholm operator $T$ the **index** of $T$ is the integer

$$\operatorname{ind}T:=\dim_{\mathbb F}\ker T-\dim_{\mathbb F}\operatorname{coker}T$$

Here subtraction is in $\mathbb Z$, not in $\mathbb N$: write $a=\dim_{\mathbb F}\ker T$ and $b=\dim_{\mathbb F}\operatorname{coker}T$ and identify a natural $n$ with $[(n,0)]$. Precisely,

$$\operatorname{ind}T=[(a,b)]=[(a,0)]+(-[(b,0)])\in\mathbb Z$$

by [[def-integers]] and [[def-int-operations]]. Both dimensions are natural numbers, so this class is defined even when $a<b$; the index may be positive, negative or zero.

**Two remarks on the definition.** The closedness of the range is listed
explicitly as a hypothesis of the definition rather than extracted from the
other clauses. And no property of the index is asserted here; additivity,
local constancy and invariance under compact perturbations are separate
theorems.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.
